title: Prompt Claude with Testable Contracts
summary: Turn a real task into a clear, structured, testable Claude prompt and improve it from evaluation evidence instead of guesswork.
objectives: Define success criteria and evaluation cases before tuning a Claude prompt.
Structure instructions, context, examples, variable input, and output requirements clearly.
Use relevant and diverse examples without leaking secrets or treating untrusted content as instructions.
Diagnose whether a failed result needs prompt, context, model, tool, or application changes.

sections.title: Define success before changing wording

sections.callout: A better-sounding response is not evidence of a better prompt. Compare both versions on the same cases and rubric.

paragraphs: State the task, audience, trusted context, constraints, required steps, output shape, and verification. If order or completeness matters, use explicit numbered instructions. sections.title: Structure context and trust boundaries
paragraphs: Separate instructions from reference documents, examples, and user-supplied variable input. Descriptive XML tags can make complex prompts easier to inspect and reduce accidental mixing of roles, especially when several documents or examples are included. code.label: Testable Claude prompt shape
code.code:
<instructions>
  Produce a decision memo using only supported claims.
</instructions>
<success_criteria>
  Include recommendation, tradeoffs, evidence links, and unresolved risks.
</success_criteria>
<context trust="authoritative">
  [APPROVED SOURCE MATERIAL]
</context>
<input trust="untrusted">
  [VARIABLE USER REQUEST]
</input>
<output_contract>
  Markdown with the required headings; label unsupported claims.
</output_contract>
<verification>
  Check every material claim against the approved context before finishing.
</verification>

sections.title: Use examples deliberately
paragraphs: Examples can demonstrate the desired format, tone, classification boundary, and edge-case behavior more precisely than abstract instructions. paragraphs: Run the original and candidate prompt against the same versioned case set. activity.title: Build and evaluate a Claude prompt contract
instructions: Choose a recurring task and define a rubric with at least four criteria, one unacceptable failure, and an 80 percent pass threshold.
Create six versioned cases: three typical, one boundary, one adversarial or instruction-conflict case, and one prior failure.
Write a prompt that separates instructions, authoritative context, untrusted input, examples, output contract, and verification.
Compare a baseline and candidate on the same cases, classify every miss, and recommend prompt, context, model, tool, or application action from the evidence.
evidence: A secret-free prompt template, rubric, and six-case evaluation set with trust boundaries and expected behavior.
A baseline-versus-candidate report with per-case scores, failure classifications, version information, and a ship, revise, or reject decision.
activity.reflectionPrompt: Which failed case could not be repaired safely by prompt wording alone, and what system boundary needed to change?

cues.text: Ask learners how an example can improve format consistency while still creating an unintended bias.
Allow three minutes to classify one miss as prompt, context, model, tool, policy, or application failure.
Check that baseline and candidate used identical cases, rubric, model configuration, and documented versions.
Guide the learner through success criteria, prompt structure, six cases, comparison, and failure classification.
Begin the check after the learner can improve a prompt from evidence without treating every failure as wording.

questions.prompt: What should exist before prompt wording is optimized?
choices: Success criteria, representative cases, a rubric, and a threshold
questions.explanation: Prompt changes need predeclared success evidence so improvement can be measured rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of XML tags in a complex Claude prompt?
choices: To organize and distinguish prompt components
questions.explanation: Tags clarify structure; external systems must still enforce trust, permissions, and validation.

questions.prompt: Which example set is most useful?
choices: One example containing a production credential
Examples copied from the hidden evaluation set
Relevant, diverse, approved examples that cover format and edge behavior
questions.explanation: Examples should represent the task and important variation without secrets or evaluation leakage.

questions.prompt: A response lacks facts that were never supplied or retrievable. What is the first failure classification?
questions.explanation: Prompt wording cannot recover authoritative information that the workflow did not make available.

questions.prompt: How should a candidate prompt be compared with its baseline?
choices: On one new demo with no rubric
On the same versioned cases, rubric, and configuration with recorded failures
By selecting the response that sounds most confident
questions.explanation: Controlled comparison and failure evidence make the prompt decision reproducible and reversible.
